articles.text: Piedmont Housing Puzzle open for public comment through May 1 The City of Piedmont has published its Draft Housing Element for the 6th Housing Cycle on the city website and Piedmontishome.org. The 374- page document, published April 8, details policies that aim to increase housing access and affordability in Piedmont. All community members, including city staff and school employees, are encouraged to review and provide comment on the draft that will be considered by City Council and Planning Commissioners. Comments received before May 5 will be considered by Planning Commissioners at the first public hearing regarding the draft housing element. “This document (Draft Housing Element) is foundational for us as a City, in regard to how we look forward to build our community for the next several years,” said Mayor Teddy Gray King at the March 24 community workshop, which included a report on the progress of work to prepare the Draft Housing Element. “Our Housing Element holds the key to many issues including our approaches to housing, greenhouse gas emissions reduction, transportation, educational opportunity, and others. Housing is fundamental to the health and well-being of any community, including Piedmont.” To review the document, visit https://www.piedmont.ca.gov/ government/city_news___notifications/draft_housing_element_ released. Comments may also be e-mailed to Piedmontishome@ piedmont.ca.gov, using the Piedmont Housing Puzzle (see below), or by mail to: Draft Housing Element, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. Interested parties may also attend the upcoming Housing Advisory Committee meeting on April 19, and/or the Planning Commission meeting on May 12. Both meetings start at 5:30 p.m. Piedmont Housing Puzzle The City has launched the Piedmont Housing Puzzle, an interactive digital tool that allows residents to choose appropriate locations in town for 587 new housing units. The deadline to provide comment is May 1. So far, over 200 Piedmont community members have participated in the tool, Piedmont Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald confirmed. The City will produce a draft of the next housing element by mid-April. “We have received approximately 90 housing plan submissions, as of [Friday, April 8], and we hope to reach even more community members. We are compiling all of the results and all of the comments from the red comment bubble feature in the Piedmont Puzzle for the Planning Commission review at their public hearing on May 12,” Macdonald said. To submit comments and suggestions before the May 1 deadline, visit: https://piedmont.abalancingact.com/housingsim.

articles.text: Parents for Educational Excellence in Piedmont, a 501(c) (4) Changes to Piedmont School District’s curriculum inspired by Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging (DEI-B) have happened, and more are in the planning stages. These changes go beyond the Humanities and Social Sciences and they negatively impact STEM subject areas. Parents may not be aware that curriculum decisions used to be made by the teachers in each of the subject areas they taught. The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) funded a position to centralize curriculum decisions and their speaker series promoted widely disputed educational pseudo-science. For PUSD there is no statistically significant difference in CAASPP academic performance between White and NonWhite (a.k.a. BIPOC) students. Distance learning during the pandemic caused a real decline in CAASPP performance, and many more Piedmont students are delaying going to college than ever before. Despite these facts, the administration is seeking principals for both Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School who will primarily comply with the district’s DEI-B agenda and are trying to hide their hiring rubric with a non-disclosure-agreement. Piedmont School District has gone to great lengths to encourage appreciating racial and cultural diversity. Racism will never be wiped out completely and doesn’t justify radical changes to the curriculum that will negatively impact educational excellence in Piedmont. The link to my CAASPP study with splits by Gender and White/ Non-White is https://harititan. com/CAASPP_Piedmont_Unified_School_District.pdf.

We read the passion narrative where Jesus is arrested and murdered by the empire. And we stop there. We intentionally do not read on to the positive end of the story. articles.text: The California Building Standards Code (California Code of Regulations, Title 24) sets statewide building code standards. Title 24, Part 6, also known as the California Building Energy Efficiency Standards or “Energy Code”, contains mandatory measures for residential buildings (single family and multi-family) and non-residential buildings and sets an energy budget for each type of building. Title 24 receives updates every three years to incorporate the latest changes in construction and technology. The latest update (2019 Energy Code) went into effect on January 1, 2020. Starting January 1, 2023, the 2022 Energy Code will go into effect. When the Energy Code is updated, all cities and counties need to adopt the new Code and any local amendments to the Code. Reach codes are local amendments that go above and beyond existing California building codes to improve the energy efficiency of buildings and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Here in Piedmont, the City Council adopted Ordinance 750 N.S., establishing reach codes in Piedmont, in February 2021. The ordinance went into effect on June 1, 2021 for low-rise residential buildings. The primary goal of the reach codes is to help Piedmont meet its Climate Action Plan (CAP) 2.0 emission reduction goals by reducing natural gas use and increasing building electrification efforts. Natural gas use in residential buildings is one of the biggest obstacles to achieving the City’s CAP 2.0 goals, consistently comprising about half of Piedmont’s in-territory emissions. Since June 1, 2021, Piedmont has made it a priority to assess the implementation of reach codes for residential buildings in Piedmont. These efforts include evaluation of building permits and the effectiveness of the policy, in addition to community outreach and engagement. This process is important to the City as staff begin to prepare for adopting the new energy code and re-adopting applicable reach code amendments. To help inform residents, City staff members are launching the 2022 reach code public engagement process. The first component is asking residents to complete an online survey to provide feedback about the current reach codes and suggestions for the next round. The online survey is live and will be open until May 20. A link to the survey can be found online at the City’s Reach Code Information page at https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ planning _ _ _building/about_ building_/reach_code_information. All those who complete the online survey will be enrolled in a raffle to receive a bill credit from Piedmont’s local electricity service provider, East Bay Community Energy (EBCE). The second component will be a Reach Code Community Forum next Wednesday, April 20, from 6:00 to 7:30 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall, 701 Highland Avenue. City staff will present an overview of Piedmont’s current reach codes, the 2022 Energy Code, and initial considerations for the next set of reach codes, followed by a community workshop where attendees will be asked to provide comments and recommendations about the current and future code. Registration for the in-person event is encouraged but not required. To register, see: https:// docs.google.com /for ms/d /e/ 1FA I p QL Sf z s K AQ32 t 2 h h - k59XZIlC8k83R8GTjocs_EvbkIQygjQmr4UQ/viewform. All attendees will be entered into a raffle to win a free energy savings kit and EBCE bill credit. For more information about the reach codes and upcoming events, visit the City’s Reach Code Information webpage. Additional information about building electrification, rebates, resources, and incentives available for Piedmonters can be found at https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ planning _ _ _building/about_ building_/electrification. Alyssa Dykman is the city’s Sustainability Program Manager. She can be reached at adykman@ piedmont.ca.gov.

Upcoming events on City’s Reach Codes By Alyssa Dykman The California Building Standards Code (California Code of Regulations, Title 24) sets statewide building code standards. Title 24, Part 6, also known as the California Building Energy Efficiency Standards or “Energy Code”, contains mandatory measures for residential buildings (single family and multi-family) and non-residential buildings and sets an energy budget for each type of building. Title 24 receives updates every three years to incorporate the latest changes in construction and technology. The latest update (2019 Energy Code) went into effect on January 1, 2020. Starting January 1, 2023, the 2022 Energy Code will go into effect. When the Energy Code is updated, all cities and counties need to adopt the new Code and any local amendments to the Code. Reach codes are local amendments that go above and beyond existing California building codes to improve the energy efficiency of buildings and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Here in Piedmont, the City Council adopted Ordinance 750 N.S., establishing reach codes in Piedmont, in February 2021. The ordinance went into effect on June 1, 2021 for low-rise residential buildings. The primary goal of the reach codes is to help Piedmont meet its Climate Action Plan (CAP) 2.0 emission reduction goals by reducing natural gas use and increasing building electrification efforts. Natural gas use in residential buildings is one of the biggest obstacles to achieving the City’s CAP 2.0 goals, consistently comprising about half of Piedmont’s in-territory emissions. Since June 1, 2021, Piedmont has made it a priority to assess the implementation of reach codes for residential buildings in Piedmont. These efforts include evaluation of building permits and the effectiveness of the policy, in addition to community outreach and engagement. This process is important to the City as staff begin to prepare for adopting the new energy code and re-adopting applicable reach code amendments. articles.text: The Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present a Zoom webinar at 6 p.m. on Thursday, May 5, entitled Power to Heal, featuring the documentary film The Power to Heal: Medicare and the Civil Rights Revolution, a film by Charles Burnett. The event will be co-hosted by the City, the Piedmont League of Women Voters, Piedmont Anti-racism Diversity Committee, and Piedmont Adult Education. The documentary highlights the genesis of Medicare, when it was signed into law, as well as its relation to the Civil Rights Revolution. The hour-long film describes the history of segregated hospitals and a brief summary of civil rights activism to the internal workings of the federal government that led to integrated hospitals and African American access to health care. It narrates the early days of health inequity, powerfully demonstrating how race and poverty denied African Americans equal access to healthcare. Included are interviews that reveal personal experiences of African Americans’ struggles with illness and death without adequate healthcare. The film transitions from these individual stories to a broader review of disparities in hospital care throughout the United States. Physicians, civil rights leaders, and historians recount the dangerous tasks of documenting egregious incidents, Dr. Neil Powe will be the speaker following the screening. tracking down patients, and the risks of blacks and whites working together to put desegregated structures in place. Following the screening, viewers will hear from Dr. Neil Powe, a leader in Public Health and the ongoing effort to correct healthcare disparities. Dr. Powe is a Harvard-trained physician, a professor of medicine at UCSF, and Chief of Medicine at San Francisco General Hospital. Viewers will hear from him about the history and current status of healthcare. He will have a question and answer session. Register for a link to stream the webinar at diversityfilmseries.org. articles.text: After five years of helping grow Piedmont Language School, Blair Paige will step down as Executive Director at the end of the school year. The PLS Board, students, and parents thank her for her time, work, and dedication in promoting world languages in Piedmont. Almost 50 years ago, a group of Piedmont parents created the independent language school, independent of Piedmont School District, in an effort to expose children at a young age to foreign languages, primarily French, Mandarin, Spanish, and Japanese. The organization grew to a size where it needed a part-time staff. PLS currently offers only Mandarin and Spanish to students in grades K-6, using classrooms at Beach, Havens, and Wildwood elementary school classrooms, in addition to the middle school and Piedmont Community Church. The Spanish curriculum and teachers are overseen by Viva el Espanol, while simplified Mandarin is taught by local teachers who have been with PLS for years. As with all schools, PLS was challenged by the COVID pandemic. This year the Spanish classes were in person, and Mandarin classes have been hybrid. Anyone interested in taking the reins to make sure the Mandarin and Spanish classes continue is asked to email piedmontlanguageschool@gmail.com.

articles.text: On March 25, School Superintendent Randy Booker spoke with the Parents’ Club about the process he intended to follow for hiring a new principal for Piedmont High School. Applications for the position were closed on March 14, and Booker said he intends to make a recommendation to the school board for the new hire at a closed session of the school board meeting on April 27. Prior to the first round of interviews, video and writing Submission were due March 23. The first round of interviews started on March 30. At the March 25 meeting with the Parents Club, Booker did not give exact numbers of applicants, indicating that there were at least seven or eight, and adding a puzzling comment; “We are going to have some community engagement opportunities moving forward.” Booker focused on the need to provide anonymity for the candidates. “That process has to be really confidential until you are a finalist. articles.text: Allyson Aleksey Arithmetic and middle school algebra are basic, right? But even parents who use advanced math in their daily lives may have trouble now helping their kids with math . The California State Board of Education adopted the Mathematics Framework on November 6, 2013 changing the way mathematics is taught. It is known as common core. What has changed? Factor trees are gone. Fractions are taught by using the “Big One” method and the all mysterious “algebra tiles” are used to build visual representations of polynomials. As a tutor I have witnessed time and again the frustration of parents because the way they teach relatively rudimentary math principals has changed. For example, long multiplication and division are now called “standard algorithm.” A parent could be driven mad by the new term M.A.D. (Mean Absolute Deviation). Often a weird new term for something basic can be the final straw for parents to look for a tutor. However, not everyone can afford a tutor or find a good fit. So, what’s another option? One technique I use if there is a disconnect between Common Core is how I learned a math method: pass the chalk to the student and let them teach. When they can teach it to someone else, they certainly will be able to “teach it to the test.” Using a big chalk board or white board can make this process fun and give students the feeling they have an arena to teach while parents, siblings or friends can sit back and watch. Don’t underestimate the power of a white board. Students can write big and get some personal space without having someone looking over their shoulder to see a small piece of paper. Letting them teach the new method may open the door for you to teach the old, tried and true way that gets to the answer as well. In sharing multiple ways, a deeper understanding can be reached. “New” method isn’t so new Teaching fourth grade Common Core mathematics in the classroom wasn’t an obstacle. Often the roadblock came when my students’ parents and guardians insisted that the “new method” was too complicated, and very foreign from the way they were taught decades ago. As a teacher, I had to reconcile with learning a different method, too. In reality, the way your child is learning is not a “new” method; it’s simply a way to encourage children to think of numbers and the amounts they represent. Instead of encouraging memorization, Common Core mathematics aims to equip students at all levels with reasoning ability. Here’s an example: a student is asked to solve 4 x 27. Anyone over the age of 25 will likely line the numbers vertically, multiply the ‘ones’ place, carry the 2, and find the product is 108. Children are now encouraged to think of the quantity the number represents. Students now solve that same problem as 4 x 25 = 100, plus 4 x 2 = 8, with both those products added together to get 108. Although the latter may seem more complicated and probably foreign, it is aimed to have a student quantify rather than memorize. Common Core standards used in California schools encourage students to explain how they figure out their answers. When you find yourself struggling to help your child with homework, ask them to show you what they know. Find an equation to solve in your child’s textbook, homework sheet or on a previous test. Write it down and tell your child that you will try to solve it, and have them solve it their way simultaneously. When you’ve both arrived at your answers, take a look and see if you’ve arrived at the same answer. Now ask them to walk you through how they worked out the problem. Polls show that Californians by-and-large support the Common Core curriculum. In 2017, former president Donald Trump led an anti-Common Core rhetoric. His Education Secretary, Betsy DeVos, called the teaching standards “dead,” but the interference was met with opposition from education leaders throughout California. For all intents and purposes, it appears that Common Core is here to stay. If you are having trouble figuring out how to solve your child’s homework, consider taking a backseat and play the role of a student. If you see your children are still struggling to explain how they work through a problem, talk with their teacher and ask them if they notice your child struggling in the classroom. Always remember that the parent-teacher team is a powerful one, and that you are both working toward one common goal. Jay Russell has over 10 years of experience as a tutor; he specializes in essay writing and algebra. Allyson Aleksey is a former 4th grade teacher at a private, accelerated school in Metairie, Louisiana.

articles.text: I recently was listening to a podcast featuring Dr. Saundra Dalton-Smith in which she was discussing the seven different kinds of rest that we need. One really stood out to me: Creative Rest. Her definition of creativity is any time we need to solve a problem. By that definition, basically every moment of parenting is an act of creativity. How do we get the kids out of the house in the morning when they are moving as slow as turtles? How can we get the siblings to stop arguing over who gets to choose the show to watch during screen time? How do we convince an unwilling child to engage in homework that is hard? All of these problems require creativity in order to solve them, and we parents are in a constant state of creative thinking. Dr. Dalton-Smith recommends that those of us who are in creative thinking mode all day every day need a rest from that kind of work and that we can find that rest through viewing beauty. That could be through seeing art in an art gallery, going to see live theatre, listening to music or spending time in nature. I realized that, in my life, pre-pandemic, I engaged in a lot of these activities–exploring a new exhibit at a museum, watching musicals and plays, going to live concerts–but all of these activities came to an abrupt halt when the shut-own started. Parents need to take creative rest in nature. Instead, I drastically increased my time in nature. Like so many of us, taking walks, going on hikes, camping, cross country skiing. . . all of these became a lifeline for me. It wasn’t until I heard this podcast that I realized that being outdoors – in the mountains, at the beach, observing wildflowers – had taken on a critical new dimension, both physical and spiritual. Now, the arts and culture sector has opened again. I am seeing shows again and it feels amazing. But I am still in nature whenever possible, and I have a newfound appreciation for the creativity and beauty of nature. • The wind in the trees is a symphony. • The sunset is a glorious painting. • Two squirrels arguing over an acorn is theater. • The movement of the waves as they crash on the shore is modern dance. As we move into the spring and summer, I want to encourage all of us parents to take the Creative Rest we need. Find the beautiful things that inspire you! Go see the shows and enjoy the exquisite nature all around us. It might just give your depleted system the rest it needs. Nina Meehan is the CEO and founder of Bay Area Children’s Theatre, currently playing “The Imaginaries: An Immersive Musical,” and the host of the Creative Parenting Podcast.

articles.text: Jan Howland (left), Nathan Walden, and children’s author Lisa Riddiough. Former Piedmont resident Lisa Riddiough recently unveiled her second children’s book, Letters to Live By: an Alphabet Book with Intention. A book-signing event was hosted by Nathan Waldon at his Nathan & Co. gift shop on Piedmont Avenue on Saturday, April 2. “Lisa is a longtime friend and we’re so excited to add Letters to Live By to our selection of children’s books,” said Waldon. “The book’s message is exactly what we look for when curating our collection: It inspires by reinforcing core values that help create a better world.” The book signing event coincided with the shop’s 16th anniversary. “What better way to celebrate? A friend, an inspiring children’s book, and cookies,” said Walden. Letters to Live By is Riddiough’s second book, illustrated by Asa Gilland. The author describes it as a social-emotional concept picture book that teaches young readers the power of setting intentions and embracing mindfulness. Letters to Live By is her debut picture book and is dedicated to Piedmont Middle School teacher Ted Greenbaum. “It is surreal to have two books out in the world,” Riddiough said. The author’s first published book, Elvis and the World as it Stands, references Letters to Live By. “When I was writing Elvis, my main character needed to refer to an alphabet book early in the story, so I used my own book. Little did I know both would be published around the same time, let alone published at all. It’s a little ‘Easter egg’ of sorts and makes the publication of both books all the sweeter,” she said. “I knew I wanted alliterative phrases that could be both intentions and action items that could be accessible to younger readers,” Letters to Live By is Lisa Riddiough’s latest children’s book. Riddiough said of the inspiration behind Letters to Live By. “I was reminded of a phrase that one of my kids’ teachers used to say. Mr. Greenebaum, of Piedmont Middle School, sends his students home at the end of each week with his signature line, ‘Rest up, have fun, read something, and practice peace.’ I first heard this at back-to-school night and, as a picture book writer, ‘Practice Peace’ stuck with me.” Riddiough said she was a slow reader as a child and found it difficult to concentrate on required reading. This led her to choose literature with plenty of illustrations and white space, “and always stories with animals,” she added. “It’s perfectly okay to choose a book that is short, has large font, and plenty of illustrations,” she said. By Allyson Aleksey Former Piedmont resident Lisa Riddiough recently unveiled her second children’s book, Letters to Live By: an Alphabet Book with Intention. A book-signing event was hosted by Nathan Waldon at his Nathan & Co. gift shop on Piedmont Avenue on Saturday, April 2. “Lisa is a longtime friend and we’re so excited to add Letters to Live By to our selection of children’s books,” said Waldon. “The book’s message is exactly what we look for when curating our collection: It inspires by reinforcing core values that help create a better world.” The book signing event coincided with the shop’s 16th anniversary. “What better way to celebrate? A friend, an inspiring children’s book, and cookies,” said Walden. Letters to Live By is Riddiough’s second book, illustrated by Asa Gilland. The author describes it as a social-emotional concept picture book that teaches young readers the power of setting intentions and embracing mindfulness. Letters to Live By is her debut picture book and is dedicated to Piedmont Middle School teacher Ted Greenbaum. “It is surreal to have two books out in the world,” Riddiough said. The author’s first published book, Elvis and the World as it Stands, references Letters to Live By. “When I was writing Elvis, my main character needed to refer to an alphabet book early in the story, so I used my own book. Little did I know both would be published around the same time, let alone published at all. It’s a little ‘Easter egg’ of sorts and makes the publication of both books all the sweeter,” she said. “I knew I wanted alliterative phrases that could be both intentions and action items that could be accessible to younger readers,” Letters to Live By is Lisa Riddiough’s latest children’s book. Riddiough said of the inspiration behind Letters to Live By. “I was reminded of a phrase that one of my kids’ teachers used to say. Mr. Greenebaum, of Piedmont Middle School, sends his students home at the end of each week with his signature line, ‘Rest up, have fun, read something, and practice peace.’ I first heard this at back-to-school night and, as a picture book writer, ‘Practice Peace’ stuck with me.” Riddiough said she was a slow reader as a child and found it difficult to concentrate on required reading. This led her to choose literature with plenty of illustrations and white space, “and always stories with animals,” she added. “It’s perfectly okay to choose a book that is short, has large font, and plenty of illustrations,” she said. His time of 9:12.62 in the 3200 meters broke Steve Brown’s record set 27 years ago in 1994 by slightly over five seconds. Brown was inducted into the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame in 2008. Stein finished 12th in a field of 82 runners. His school record comes one week after setting the school’s 11-year old record in the 1600 meters at the Stanford Invitational. You have competition from all over the country there. It’s a great experience, I remember going into the tent and everyone is asking each other where they are from. I think runners from 29 states were there,” said Stein. He entered the race just three seconds behind Brown’s all-time record after running a 9:20.56 at the Stanford Invitational. Stein knew that Arcadia would be the perfect setting to break it. In doing so, he ran a 4:37 in his first mile and a 4:35 to close. “Many heats were coming out really fast. articles.text: On April 5, Piedmont High School senior Parker Terrill was awarded a commemorative beltbuckle for setting a new school record in the pole vault. Terrill’s vault of 15 feet, 5 inches, broke Marshall Wentworth’s record set 11 years ago by 1 foot, 5 inches. The brass buckle with a raised image of a pole vaulter was given to Wentworth by the family of Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame inductee Irving Moore, whose record of 13-feet was set in 1940. According to coach Jeanine Holmlund, the buckle was given to Wentworth with the understanding that he would pass it on to the next school record holder. It is now Terrill’s duty to pass it onto the school’s next record holder when and if it occurs. articles.text: Editor: I read about the incredible performances by Ellie Black, Jack Stein, and Parker Terrill at this year’s Arcadia Invitational. Terrill’s 6th place finish in the Invitational Pole Vault and Black’s 3rd place finish in the Rated 3200 Meter Race were exceptional. But it was Stein’s performance I had my eye on. It was with mixed emotions that I read that he broke my school record for 3200 meters. I suppose records are meant to be broken and mine was no different. School records aren’t broken every day, though. The one I broke was set by Tim Tyler in 1970. My school record was set at the 1994 CIF State Track & Field Championships. I came in 12th, running 9:17.71. The winner that day was Mebrahtom Keflezighi who went on to win the Silver Medal in the 2004 Olympic Marathon. There was once a video of the race on YouTube and if you had the patience to wait for a while, you could see me crossing the finish line 20 seconds after him. It took years for it to sink in what an honor it was to compete in such an elite prep race. High school distance running is now at a completely different level than when I competed. I am blown away by the outstanding performances of this generation’s athletes. I hope Arcadia is a preview of things to come for Stein this season and beyond. I hope he takes as much pride in his new record as I did in mine. Leaving that aside, I hope he finds as much joy running as I have. Above all, I hope that the next generation of Piedmont athletes looks at that record, 9:12.62 or faster if Stein breaks the record again, and trains a little harder, dreams a little bigger, and thinks, ‘Records are meant to be broken and this one is no different. Why shouldn’t I be the one to break it?’ Steve Brown, PHS Class of ‘94 Oberlin, Ohio

articles.text: The PHS girls’ lacrosse team honored its 10 seniors on its roster last Tuesday, April 5 at Witter Field, shutting out Western Alameda County Conference opponent Moreau Catholic of Hayward 18-0. articles.text: Nico Defazio went 2-for-3 with two RBIs, a walk, and a stolen base against St. Mary’s. The Piedmont High baseball team traveled to St. Mary’s in Berkeley on Friday, April 8, losing 4-2 in a defensive battle with a former longtime rival. The Panthers are a Division 4 opponent in North Coast Section, and the two sides could certainly meet each other once again in the postseason. The pair of games brings PHS’ record to 8-6 overall heading into Spring Break. The Highlanders started strong with one run in the top of the first inning but fell behind 3-1 by the next inning. PHS narrowed the gap to 3-2 in the top of the firth, but St. Mary’s tacked on one more in the bottom half of the fifth. In the top of the first, Piedmont had two runners on base with two outs after Peter Krumins and Davis Alazraqui were hit by pitches. Nico Defazio hit a ground ball through the infield to score Krumins from third. PHS had runners in scoring position in the top of the second after Liam Campbell and Michael Aikawa recorded singles, but a double play ended the inning. St. Mary’s answered with three runs in the bottom half of the second inning, scoring two with two outs after hitting a single and triple. The Highlanders closed the deficit to 3-2 in the top of the fifth with Alazraqui drawing a walk and advancing to second on a wild pitch. Defazio cracked a single to center to score Alazraqui all the way from first. Defazio Third baseman Peter Krumins with a throw to second. advanced to second on the throw. But the Highlanders couldn’t bring him to score. St. Mary’s rallied for its fourth run in the bottom half after their leadoff hitter walked and stole second, advancing to third on a sacrifice bunt. With one out, the Panthers brought him in on a sacrifice fly to right field for the 4-2 final. St. Mary’s forced a 1-2-3 inning in the top of the sixth. In Piedmont’s final opportunity in the top of the seventh, St. Mary’s struck out the side. Final stats: Defazio went 2-for-3 with two RBIs, a walk, and a stolen base. Aikawa went 1-for-4. Krumins had a run scored. Alazraqui had a run scored and drew two walks. Campbell went 1-for-3. Alex Tafapolsky got the start on the mound, throwing five innings and striking out three with one earned run. Scott McKenzie pitched one inning in relief and struck out two. articles.text: Playwright Dave Malloy, a three-time Tony Award nominee, makes his debut at Berkeley Rep with Octet, beginning April 20. Directed by Annie Tippe, the show features a score for an a cappella chamber choir and an original libretto inspired by internet comment boards, scientific debates, religious texts, and Sufi poetry. Octet explores addiction and nihilism within the messy context of 21st century technology. It was commissioned, developed, and produced by Signature Theatre in New York City, and follows the lives of eight “internet-obsessed” people who meet in real life to share their stories, using nothing but a pitch pipe and a cappella voices. Or Matias is music director. The cast includes Kim Blanck, Adam Bashian, Alex Gibson, Justin Lopez, J.D Mollison, Kuhoo Verma, Margo Seibert, and Isabel Santiago. articles.text: Berkeley-based Shotgun Players is presenting Passing Strange live through April 23. Passing Strange is directed by William Thomas Hodgson with music direction by Daniel Alley. The play follows the story of a young Bohemian who charts a course for “the real,” through sex, drugs and rock and roll. The play is set in middle-class America, Amsterdam, and Berlin. Passing Strange won a Tony Award for Best Book of a Musical. “Watching Passing Strange changed me, changed what my art could be. I just saw myself in this.” said Hodgson. “There’s just something about the rock nature of this where I’m just having such a good time. And I don’t always feel that in the theatre. The commune between the actors, the musicians, and the audience: it feels like centering that in a theatre experience is sometimes what I’m missing from my theatre experience. There’s something that’s so accessible in this play, in the writing.” The cast includes Angel Adedokun, Rolanda Bell, Myles Brown, Devin Cunningham, and Albert Hodge. articles.text: Mendocino Music Festival returns live this summer, beginning July 9 at Cotton Auditorium in Fort Bragg. Tickets are on sale now. The festival was established in 1986 by Allan Pollack, Susan Waterfall and former principal bassoonist of the San Francisco Symphony, Walter Green. The festival features a blend of genres; evenings include orchestral concerts, Big Band, chamber music ensembles, dance, blues, jazz, world, folk, bluegrass and more. Daytime events include lectures and recitals at the Piano Series, a performance by participants in the Emerging Artists Program, and small concerts in intimate venues throughout the historic town of Mendocino on the coast. To see a full list of all events, see: https://mendocinomusic.org/ events/2022-07/. The featured artists and bands this year include Steel Wheels, Spencer Myer, Gloria Cheng, and Kim Nalley. Proof of vaccination will be required for entry. Masks must be properly worn while on event premises, and concerts will be limited to one hour with no intermission. The festival will follow official recommendations of local and state public health agencies as July approaches. Mendocino Music Festival concerts will take place this summer in the Cotton Auditorium in Fort Bragg.

articles.text: Dan Flanagan is a Berkeley violinist who currently teaches violin at UC Berkeley, is Principal Second of the Berkeley Symphony, Concertmaster of the Sacramento Philharmonic and Opera, Concertmaster of West Edge Opera, and performs with the San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Ballet. He has previously performed as concertmaster with Oakland Symphony, California Symphony, Symphony San Jose, Santa Rosa Symphony, California Musical Theater, Modesto Symphony, and Opera Parallele. He has performed recitals at the Piedmont Center for the Arts multiple times. Dan has been an avid collector since he discovered baseball cards at the age of five. He lost interest in them as a teenager but with the advent of Ebay when he was in grad school, he amassed an impressive collection of historical violinist memorabilia. When he moved to Berkeley 12 years ago, he discovered art auctions and open studios; that’s when the real trouble started. Since then his focus has been French Impressionists and Bay Area abstracts. The works on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts include 45 of his favorite pieces. Many of the artists were in the original Impressionist exhibits of the 1870’s and 1880’s. Dan has a project titled “The Bow and the Brush,” where he performs new compositions inspired by paintings. Two of these pieces were performed in the Berkeley Symphony & Friends Chamber Concert series on April 10. Twenty-one of these works, each inspired by paintings currently exhibited at the Piedmont Center for the Arts ere, will be premiered by Dan at his Carnegie Hall debut on October 3, followed by the West Coast premieres at Hertz Hall in Berkeley on October 16. Robert Antoine Pinchon (French, 1886-1943). Bruxelles, pluie sur la Grand-Place (Brussels, rain on the Grand-Place), Oil on canvas, 1928. Jose Gonzalez Garcia composed “Cadenza II,” inspired by this painting.

articles.text: “No Strings Attached.” Right. The ending of this movie was telegraphed in the first 20 minutes. It was just a matter of waiting and enduring the following 90 minutes while two 20-somethings, Emma (Natalie Portman) and Adam (Ashton Kutcher), who’ve decided to be friends with benefits (sex buddies, no strings attached), begin what is loosely called a relationship. Their intent is disclosed via a lengthy montage of urgent groping and coupling in hospital storage rooms, an empty operating theater, her apartment, and his house. Ground rule: rinse and repeat. Adam, breaking one of the fundamental rules of their encounters, concludes he is falling in love with Emma. She, however, is opposed to any attachments that go beyond the physical. In other words, she’s commitment adverse and “no strings” is a metaphor, of sorts, for a personality disorder that is completely inexplicable. Of course, there’s not one person in the audience that believes that she will not completely reassess her position by act three, and “No Strings Attached” will suddenly have lots of strings. And while we’re on the subject of strings, sticking with this movie through the credits is like trying to push string. Meanwhile, because Emma and Adam are intent on not building a relationship, they avoid any and all conversations that might involve self-disclosure. No issues are raised. Hence, little if anything is known about them as people. In fact, they are emotional strangers to one another. There is Adam’s dad, Alvin (Kevin Kline), a pot smoking, skirt chasing (under 30), fading television star who is in denial when it comes to the fact that he is old. His character is needless and silly. For Kline, a superb actor, this role has a very short shelf life and he walks through it with a “what, me worry?” grin and little else. The dialogue, such as it is, that moves the film forward, is coarse and crude and vacuous. This may be a generational thing, but tell me that this is not the way young people interact. Nature abhors a vacuum, but not Hollywood. They’ve created the contemporary romantic comedy, a seemingly endless string of them over the last several years, all formulaic, predictable, many similar in plot (“No Strings Attached” brings to mind the recent “Love and Other Drugs”). Think of Hollywood as some kind of rom-com Pez dispenser and just when you thought it was safe to go back into the movie theater, another shallow, existential black hole of a film appears. “No Strings Attached” could have been an interesting film. There is a qualitative difference between hooking up with someone and actually wanting to know them. Just Emma’s deep-seated fear of relationships offers the prospect of a story line that might have yielded something deeper than the banal and the nonsensical. Adam and Emma have backstory, they have careers. Adam wants desperately to be a writer; however, he never so much as shares a word he’s written with Emma. Emma is working 36-hour shifts to be a doctor, and obviously cares about people; however we never hear her touch on her motivations for wanting to care for people. Of course, they’re busy not talking, not disclosing, not reflecting – to the detriment of their relationship and the film. No Strings Attached. Starring Ashton Kutcher, Natalie Portman, Olivia Thirlby and Greta Gerwig. Directed by Ivan Reitman. 2 hrs., 34 min. Rated R. Review originally published in 2011. articles.text: If you love movies, then it’s likely you’ve heard of director Peter Weir. Now 68-years-old, his work dates back to 1975 and the chilling Australian film, Picnic at Hanging Rock, followed by The Year of Living Dangerously, Gallipoli, Witness, Dead Poets Society, The Truman Show, The Mosquito Coast, and the incomparable Master and Commander, shot in 2003 and based on the Patrick O’Brian stories. The Way Back has an epic feel, and it transcends what may, at first blush, seem a rudimentary plot: the year is 1940 and a rag tag group of men improbably escape a Russian gulag work camp. Against all odds they trek more than 4,000 miles across some of the most inhospitable country imaginable. Their destination, as it turns out, is British-controlled India. This is not a road trip. It is not simply about walking. This is a film, shot by the deeply talented cinematographer, Russell Boyd, celebrates the human spirit, and the unrelenting will of these individuals to not only endure but to prevail, and, in the end, be free. Not all will survive, we’re told at the outset; however, each character – Janusz (Jim Surgess), Mr. Smith (Ed Harris), Valka (Colin Farrell), Tamasz (Alexandru Potocean), Irena (Saoirse Ronan) – becomes three dimensional as does the landscape, which conspires to defeat them. They escape Siberia; find, against all odds, Lake Baikal; cross the plains of Mongolia; survive the heat and sandstorms of the Ghobi Desert; and face the snows and spires of the Himalayas, the gateway to Tibet. Beyond is India. How they accomplish this remarkable feat makes for an astonishing tale, not unlike, in some strange way, the survival tale, 127 Hours. Both experiences are testimony to the depth of the very human desire to survive. While 127 Hours is relatively static and claustrophobic, The Way Back is all about movement and space, filling the screen with vistas that are startling in their seemingly benign beauty, though clearly malevolent in their raw harshness and inherent deprivations. The performances by the international ensemble are outstanding, led by Harris as a stoic American engineer who came to Moscow in the 1930s with this teenage son to work on Moscow’s Metro. During a purge, his son is killed and he is sent to the gulag. Sturgess portrays Janusz, a young Polish cavalry officer, accused by his wife of spying. And there’s Farrell’s fine performance as the gangster who cannot connect Stalin’s “reign of terror” to his own incarceration. Ronan is perfect as Irena, a young girl who finds the group weeks after they have escaped and joins them on their journey. The film belies the theory that January (with the exception of late Oscar releases) is caught in the movie doldrums. This Peter Weir film, if it portends anything, is hopefully the first of other fine films to follow. The Way Back. Directed by Peter Weir. Starring Jim Sturgess, Ed Harris, Colin Farrell, Mark Strong, and Saoirse Ronan. 2 hrs., 13 min. Rated PG-13. Released and originally reviewed in the Post in 2011.
articles.title: The Way Back a fine film by Peter Weir

articles.text: A scene from the 2015 Oscar nominated animated film Shaun the Sheep. Shaun the Sheep Movie, the 2015 Oscar nominated claymation animated feature film from the British Aardman Studios of Wallace and Gromit fame, is now streaming on HBO Max/Prime. It’s a winning family movie, absent any intelligible dialogue (lots of facial expressions, grunts and pointing), delivered in the spirit of Buster Keaton. The story begins when Shaun, a free-spirited sheep, who lives with his flock on the Mossy Bottom Farm owned by a local farmer (John Sparkes). Shaun decides that life on the Mossy Bottom, which includes three boorish pigs, a bull and some ducks is decidedly monotonous. And so he and his wooly compatriots make a plan to keep the farmer sound asleep in his trailer, counting his sheep. Meanwhile, they are going to spend the day in the farmer’s house eating snacks and watching TV. Of course, things don’t go exactly as planned, and the trailer rolls away with the sleeping farmer, and his faithful dog Blitzer, inside. It ends up in the big city. Along the way, the farmer gets a knock on the head, and wakes up in the city hospital with a case of amnesia. Then comes a flashback to a time some 500 years earlier when the magical land of Kumandra prospered with humans and friendly dragons living in remarkable harmony. If you qualify for subsidies, the premiums for your coverage may be similar to employer-sponsored coverage; if not, though, they can be more expensive. For information on ACA Marketplace plans, visit www.healthcare.gov. If you have options for health insurance, you’ll want to take into account differences in coverage and cost. Check whether your desired health care providers are in-network and try to determine if your current medications and the benefits you rely on are covered. You may also want to consider a plan that allows you to open a health savings account (HSA), which offers potential tax benefits. Setting up a dogfriendly egg hunt in your yard is an easy way to test your dog’s sense of smell – and wear them out, too. Here are some tips for doing it yourself: 1. Some people say use hard boiled eggs out of the freezer, 2 eggs per dog, but my vote is to put their fav treat into the same cheap, plastic Easter eggs you bought for your kids and teach them to hunt them. Remember you must help the dogs open them up—no cracking the plastic. We don’t want any plastic getting into the intestinal tract. 2. Another option is to just hide treats around the yard in small paper bowls – they’ll be happy either way. Some people tie balloons to the treats in case the dog or the human needs help finding them. It’s easier for eventual clean up, too. We always found an egg a month or so later in the yard that the kids hadn’t found. 3. The best treats for an Egg Hunt are the smelly ones – the smellier the better. Dogs with more advanced noses (retrievers & Labs) will be happy with a tiny doggy biscuit placed in an egg. But if you have a Frenchie or a Bulldog, they may not get the sniffing idea. Help them out a bit; show them an egg with a smelly treat. Xylitol-free peanut butter is always a good one. Eventually they will understand that eggs mean treats. If they don’t just keep showing them. Ideas for treats are freeze-dried liver, small squares of cheese, tiny pieces of chicken jerky, cubes of cooked chicken, or regular old kibble. 4. While most dogs are not totally color-blind, bright pink won’t help them. So don’t worry about egg colors. If your grandchild loves pink, keep the pink ones away from the doggies. 5. If you want real Martha Stewart points, put bunny ears over their ears and send us pics. 6. Fenced yards are a must. If I hear of any Hunts, I will let you know but right now, it looks like you’ll be doing the Hunt in your yard. This is all good nose work. articles.text: A robust group of 28 individuals and one K-9 best friend showed up for a Walking on Wednesdays excursion on April 6: Stella Houston, Rob Smith, Pat Sheehan, Sherry Jacobs, Albert Chen, Priscilla Wanerus, Melba Yee, Lois Price, Dena Belinkoff, Claudia Lopez, Pat McMahon, Lynn Richmond, Bob Wong, Kat Lang, Alicia Rivera, Jo Normington with K-9 best friend Penny Lane, Adrienne Hamlin, Elizabeth Richter, Quincy Dong, Pat Keller, Mike Henn, Jim Kuo, Sarah Johnson, Elane Rehr, Harriette Louie, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Elane Rehr and Pat Keller brought their husbands, Howard Davis and Greg Keller. On Wednesday, April 6, Lois Price informed members of the Walking on Wednesdays group it was “National Walking Day,” a designation created in 2007 by the American Heart Association on the first April Wednesday of every year. The group was reminded that on April 20 and 27 Hope Salzer will lead sneak preview tours of two Piedmont gardens that are part of the 18th Annual “Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour and Green Home Features Showcase.” And after that, on May 4, former Piedmont mayor Bob McBain will host the walkers on a visit to Tyson Lake at the back of his Sotelo Avenue home. With the weather on the warm side last week, it was thought that it would be good to avoid a long walk with lots of climbing. Going through the center of town to Coaches Field and Kennelly Skate Park off Moraga Avenue was a level, relatively short walk. To keep the group refreshed on Piedmont history, they were reminded that Walter Blair, the first European settler in the area in 1852, had originally named this road “Vernal Avenue” because it was so lush with vegetation. When the group got to the end of Highland (Vernal) at Moraga Avenue, more of Blair’s history from Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research was shared. This included the fact that across the street on Moraga was the original entrance to Blair Park in 1884. This was Blair’s large, picnic park attraction that generated ridership for his Piedmont Railway horsecars. The group walked over the boardwalk along Moraga that spans the edge of the canyon below, and serves as a sidewalk to Coaches Field. In the parking lot in front of the field more of the area’s history was shared. This was once Piedmont’s landfill before the canyon of what is now Coaches Field was filled. The park was first dedicated in 1994; and in 2001, with the support of Piedmont native and Otis Spunkmeyer Cookies founder Ken (Bebe) Rawlings, the sports field was created. It honors the many Piedmont coaches who have worked with the city’s youth. A copy of the City Council-approved Coaches Field Expansion Concept Plan map was also shared with the walkers. The project is unfunded but is what the City would like to do with the field some day. The next destination was the Kennelly Skate Park, just beyond the left field and up a hill. With some trepidation they admired the deep bowls that much younger people fearlessly skate up and down. Most of the walkers did manage to descend some stairs that led into one of the bowls for a group photo. Though a little scary, the concrete bowls are impressive. From the skate park the walkers had a view of San Francisco and the Salesforce Tower in the distance. On the way back they admired front yards, one of which had an orchid plant that was about as big as a mid-sized Christmas tree, as well as beautiful bougainvillea and wisteria flowers. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome by registering with the Piedmont Recreation Department at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group, sponsored by Piedmont Recreation Department, met outside the Tea House in Piedmont Park on April 4 for a discussion of its April selection, Destiny of the Republic by Candice Millard. Eighteen members of the group were on hand to enjoy the beautiful weather and the book. Carol Long and Alicia Rivera continued to spoil the group with chocolate and fruit treats that added fuel to the conversation. Destiny of the Republic is Millard’s 2011 book that tells the story of the life and assassination of James A. Garfield, the 20th President of the United States. However, it is a three-way biography of President Garfield, Charles Guiteau, the president’s assassin, and inventor Alexander Graham Bell. Most Americans know little about President Garfield. Sadly, it is a story with a tragic ending. Garfield may have been one of the most extraordinary men ever elected president. He was born into poverty, but through his hard work and outstanding abilities, he became a scholar, a Civil War hero, and an admired reformist congressman. He was nominated for president against his will and fought against the corrupt political establishment of the time. However, four months after his inauguration, a deranged, federal government office seeker, Charles Guiteau, tracked Garfield down and on July 2, 1881 shot him in the back. However, the bullet didn’t kill Garfield. Doctors soon arrived on the scene and, as was common practice of the day, probed the wound with unsterilized fingers and instruments. Garfield was moved to the White House where Dr. D. Willard Bliss took charge. Bliss continued to probe the wound looking for the bullet and administering archaic treatments with disastrous effect. As the president’s condition worsened, Alexander Graham Bell, the inventor of the telephone, came to help. He worked around the clock trying to invent a new device that could find the bullet, but Bliss created obstacles and Bell was not successful. Garfield died on September 19, 1881, at the age of 49. In the autopsy, doctors discovered that Garfield had died of infection. The bullet was on the opposite side of his body from Bliss’ diagnosis. The bullet had hit no vital organs. In truth, it was Bliss’s negligence that killed Garfield, but Guiteau was convicted of murder, and hanged on June 30, 1882. The readers unanimously enjoyed Destiny of the Republic. Some “loved” Millard’s work and passed it on to family members. The group felt that the book reads like a novel and is filled with interesting details about these historical figures. The readers were impressed by the research that Millard did and all the book’s footnotes. Some readers liked Millard’s use of quotes by Garfield at the start of each chapter, showing his intellect and character. The spoil system of American politics and the process at the time to select presidential candidates were disappointing for the readers. It was also surprising how primitive the state of medical science was at the end of the 19th Century. The readers were appalled by the details of Bliss’ conduct and his mistreatment of the president. Millard made this period come alive for the readers. The group discussed how some historians have the ability to do this with characters and details that support their main story, while other non-fiction writers can clutter their works with tangential, tedious information. The group spent most of their time discussing Garfield and Bell, but finally did talk about Guiteau, the shooter. He was an unfortunate person, who today would probably be found to be too crazy to be executed. The group noted that a new book from Millard, River of the Gods, will be released in May. With their discussion complete, the readers turned to future book selections. They had previously picked the novel The Lincoln Highway by Amor Towles for May, and added The Body, a non-fiction by British-American author Bill Pryson for June, and Cloud Cuckoo Land by Pulitzer-prize winning fiction author Anthony Doerr for July. The next discussion will be Monday, May 2 at 1:30 p.m. at the Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required by calling the Recreation Department at 420-3070. First Monday Reading Group members at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. articles.text: Kathleen “Kathy” Cutter Shelly, a beloved wife, mother, grandmother, and active member of Corpus Christi and St. Joseph’s Catholic Churches, passed away on March 5, 2022 at Washington Hospital in Fremont surrounded by her loving husband and children after a valiant 7-month battle with cancer. She was 75. The daughter of Joseph (né Antonio) “Duke” Reboli and Katherine “Becky” Bannon. Kathy was born on November 16, 1946 at a premature weight of 4 pounds, 13 ounces in Oakland, California. Kathleen Anne Reboli grew up within the protective confines of her parents’ Irish-Italian household, which sat atop her grandfather C.P. Bannon’s mortuary. With a mother as an accomplished pianist and organist, Kathy often kept her company, sitting at her feet while she played for both the mortuary and local Catholic churches. The experiences greatly influenced Kathy’s love of classical, opera, and sacred music. Kathy’s mother also played music for the likes of Charlie Chaplin and other actors in silent films, including playing the pipe organ at the Grand Lake Theater in Oakland At one point she was the youngest member of the Musician’s Guild. At the time, she had broken a number of glass ceilings, having learned piano and helped to support her family from the age of 5 as a woman in the entertainment business. Kathy’s mother had a successful career into her 40s, prior to establishing a family after the birth of Kathy. She also influenced Kathy’s career-minded views and her later retirement at age 70. Kathy’s father was a professional golf instructor at the Claremont Country Club and had retired as the head golf professional at the Richmond Country Club. He volunteered during both World Wars, and was stationed on the U.S.S. Yorktown, known as “the Fighting Lady,” which was found on the Pacific Floor 56 years after it sunk. Throughout her childhood, Kathy endured multiple corrective procedures and leg braces in order help her walk. A born fighter, she eventually was able to rollerskate competitively in San Leandro and across California, with practice often beginning in the predawn hours before high school. She attended St. Bernard’s grade school and Notre Dame High School in the Bay Area. Working at Highland Hospital before becoming a collections deputy for Alameda County, Kathy subsequently worked in the telecommunications and cellular field for over 30 years, a time when pay phones were more prevalent than cell phones. Kathy was a also single mother for several years prior to meeting her beloved husband Stephen “Steve” Doyle Shelly in 1982 on a blind date. The couple was married in 1983 and would have celebrated their 39th anniversary this May. The couple began its journey in a house Kathy co-designed – a glass house on steel girders that in the 1970’s sat on a terrarium housing a cougar named “Cynthia.” Steve adopted Kathy’s children Terésa and Duke as his own, taking care of them while Kathy worked long hours and went back to school to complete a Master’s degree in Psychology at John F. Kennedy University while working full-time and commuting. Steve brought into the marriage his own son Mark, whom Kathy considered as her eldest son. In Piedmont and Fremont, where they split their time during their golden years, they were surrounded by family, neighbors, and friends who became lifelong connections. Kathy and Steve were frequent visitors at Corpus Christi Church with their granddaughter, Élodie, who remembers those Sundays fondly. The grandparents also served St. Joseph’s-Mission San Jose parish and gave back to the Catholic Church and community at large, including sponsoring the upbringing of several children around the world. Kathy was known by many for her pilgrimages to the Vatican and the churches of Croatia, Italy, and Ireland, pilgrimages that she also shared with her family and grandchildren. Kathy also became a minister of communion and RCIA teacher for several years, as well as spending time volunteering at a shelter for battered women. She later helped raise awareness for the victims of sexual trafficking. She was known for her inner strength, principles, and great faith, inspiring many to turn to prayer, even touching those who cared for her during her valiant battle with cancer. Kathleen walked in the steps of her faith throughout her life and illness, suffering and giving up her life during this Lenten season. We look forward to her resurrection during the Easter season. Kathy is survived by her husband, Steve Shelly, children Terésa Cutter Nordenfelt, Duke Cutter, and Mark Shelly, and grandchildren Killian Shelly, Keegan Shelly, Natalie Nordenfelt, Oliver Nordenfelt, Joseph Cutter, and Élodie Nordenfelt.

pages.text: Wednesday, April 13, 2022 27 Cozy corners to inspire connection By Laura Martin Bovard Much of the lifestyle we became accustomed to before we were blindsided by a pandemic has transformed. I joke with one of my beloved clients that I have learned the art of pivoting due to her sometimes quickly changing mind. My ability to pivot has also been fortified from the rapidly changing industry of building materials and furnishings brought on by the pandemic. It feels like emotional whiplash learning and subsequently delivering news about delays and discontinued items with clients. Were it not for my robust spiritual practice, I would be catatonic dealing with the stress of this industry, not to mention the heartbreak in the world today and the emotional fallout of being a mom, a wife, a friend, and a business owner. The most heart-centered way I can move forward is to focus on creating beautiful home spaces that encourage our clients’ families to gather. Gathering presents itself differently for many of our clients, so we take that into account when designing their spaces. The Bay Area is teeming with foodies and home chefs who adore a well-appointed kitchen. A sitting area keeps friends and family out of the way while creating an invitation for everyone to participate in the theater of cooking. The breakfast nook is an ideal way to accomplish that and serves even more purposes. Whether preparing and enjoying a meal, doing homework, reading a magazine, or playing Wordle, a nook is the pandemic’s answer to staying close and modernizing the dining experience. More and more, I hear stories from friends and clients about how they are beginning to see friends again. I see how humanizing that is. One underlying theme I hear most is that we are all holding our beloveds a little closer, and lingering in hugs a little longer. Witnessing the atrocities happening in Ukraine invites us to remember that nothing in life is guaranteed. The highlight of my weekend was receiving a text from a client who shared that they were enjoying their atrium with friends. “The room feels warm and wonderful and playful,” he wrote. How does it get any better than that?! (Thank you, Chris!) It can be difficult to feel gratitude instead of guilt when we are blessed with so much. However, as many wise people have reflected, feeling bad for others does not make their situation better. In fact, recognizing gratitude and meaning in our own lives is the best thing we can do to keep us out of fear and inaction.
